n0001.title: Cargo Cult Science
n0001.gist: Honest science requires reporting all evidence against your own ideas, not just what supports them.
n0001.question: Cargo Cult Science — what separates real science from empty imitations that never deliver results? (a core principle)

n0002.title: Surveying Pseudoscience
n0002.gist: Feynman surveys widespread pseudoscience—from mysticism to failed education methods—to show how easily people accept ideas that never actually work.
n0002.question: Pseudoscience — why do so many unproven beliefs persist even in a scientific age? (a survey of examples)

n0003.title: Opening and Framing
n0003.gist: This commencement address introduces Feynman's theme: how to recognize science that merely imitates genuine scientific method.

n0008.title: Investigating Mysticism and UFOs
n0008.gist: Feynman recounts personal investigations into UFOs, mysticism, extrasensory perception, and psychic claims like Uri Geller's, finding none of them actually work under scrutiny.

n0014.title: Failures in Education and Justice
n0014.gist: Even respected fields like education and criminal justice function like pseudoscience, showing no real progress despite elaborate theories, leaving ordinary people intimidated by false expertise.

n0018.title: The Cocktail Party Test
n0018.gist: Feynman proposes a cocktail party test: if a topic feels safe to discuss without embarrassment, it's probably one nobody truly understands scientifically.

n0021.title: The Cargo Cult Metaphor
n0021.gist: Feynman names Cargo Cult Science for work that mimics science's form but lacks the integrity of reporting evidence against one's own claims.
n0021.question: Cargo Cult Science — what essential quality is missing even when research looks scientific? (one core principle)

n0022.title: The Cargo Cult
n0022.gist: Feynman compares failed pseudoscience to the Pacific islanders' Cargo Cults, who built fake airstrips and control towers expecting planes to land, imitating form without substance.

n0024.title: Defining Scientific Integrity
n0024.gist: Scientific integrity means leaning over backwards to report every fact that might disprove your own theory, not only the evidence supporting it, so others can judge fairly.

n0028.title: Contrast With Advertising
n0028.gist: Feynman contrasts true scientific honesty with advertising, using Wesson Oil's technically true but misleading claim to show how omitted context can still deceive.

n0030.title: Truth Will Out
n0030.gist: Experiments eventually reveal the truth regardless of temporary fame, so lacking this scientific integrity is exactly what prevents cargo cult research from ever succeeding.

n0033.title: Learning Not to Fool Yourself
n0033.gist: The history of measuring the electron's charge shows how scientists unconsciously biased their results toward an earlier, flawed value instead of correcting it outright.
n0033.question: Self-deception — how do scientists unintentionally bias their own results toward expected answers? (a historical example)

n0034.title: Millikan's Oil-Drop Experiment
n0034.gist: Millikan's famous oil-drop experiment measuring the electron's charge contained a small error due to an incorrect value for air's viscosity.

n0036.title: Gradual Correction of the Error
n0036.gist: Later scientists, influenced by Millikan's authority, gradually and unconsciously inched their measurements toward the correct value instead of reporting large corrections immediately, revealing a subtle self-deception.

n0039.title: Honesty in Science
n0039.gist: Scientific integrity requires being honest with the public, publishing all results whether favorable or not, and resisting institutional pressure to report only convenient findings.
n0039.question: Honesty in science — what obligations do scientists have to the public and to publishing inconvenient results? (several examples)

n0040.title: Not Fooling the Layman
n0040.gist: Scientists owe laymen a stricter kind of honesty than everyday morality requires, meaning they must explain their work's real applications even if funding suffers as a result.

n0044.title: Publishing Every Result
n0044.gist: True scientific integrity demands publishing results regardless of outcome, since selectively publishing favorable findings—as in advertising or politically convenient government advice—misleads rather than informs.

n0047.title: Skipping Replication in Psychology
n0047.gist: A psychology student was discouraged from first replicating an existing experiment before testing a new variable, revealing a troubling norm against verifying prior results.

n0051.title: Pressure in Accelerator Research
n0051.gist: At a major accelerator, researchers reused mismatched old hydrogen data rather than conducting proper comparison experiments, pressured by funding needs to produce new results quickly.

n0053.title: Rigor, Neglect, and Closing
n0053.gist: A careful rat experiment that eliminated every false cue shows what true scientific rigor requires, yet later researchers ignored its lessons, much like flawed ESP research avoiding repeatability.
n0053.question: Rigor in experiments — what does real scientific care look like, and why do later researchers avoid it? (two case studies)

n0054.title: Young's Rat Experiment
n0054.gist: Psychologist Young painstakingly eliminated every possible sensory cue—sight, smell, sound—so that rats could only succeed by truly learning the maze, setting a model for rigorous experimental control.

n0059.title: Neglect of Young's Findings
n0059.gist: Despite demonstrating the proper way to run such experiments, Young's rigorous methods were ignored by later researchers, who repeated sloppy rat experiments without his careful controls.

n0061.title: ESP and Repeatability
n0061.gist: Parapsychology experiments on ESP show shrinking effects under scrutiny and resist demands for repeatability, even training students only to produce the desired psychic results.

n0064.title: Closing Wish
n0064.gist: Feynman closes with a wish for scientific freedom and a reminder to speak only when you know clearly what you mean to say.
